> https://hex.tech/

that is one of the most unhinged landing pages i've ever seen, it looks like a vibe coded claude mess that somehow raised 100M

is no one looking at what they're releasing anymore? do people just not care? i guess they don't have to if some intern can just prompt "make cool website for our useless company" and then 100M appears at your door from eager VCs

I think the hardest thing for me is all these sites and services coming out with phrases like: “Trust and govern every answer” or “Bring BI to where people work” or “self-serve in plain language” or “Trust and control behind every answer”

I’m like, what the f*k. We’re busy doing this shit for a little-hundred-mil?

Do we REALLY need these little guide notebooks? Everyone has AI just, I dunno, stuff the shit in SQLite and generate a graph.

One more thing: how many f*king insights do companies need? This shit is like analysis paralysis.

Keep it simple people, don’t pay for this crap. If you need to gather all your little magical documents, maybe it’s time to consider cleaning out the attic instead.

the best part is how they don't help at all for the hard part (collecting and curating high quality data) and instead help with the part any intern with python and a stem undergraduate could have done already (make a pretty graph)

armed with the free version of chatgpt, pretty much anyone capable of understanding or composing the question can summon such a graph nowadays, given the data.
I think it looks cool.

The massive lag and jitter as I try to scroll down doesn't feel very cool. It somehow gets better a few screens down, but still...

Worst of all they committed the cardinal sin of hijacking scrolling. Please for the love of god do not hijack scrolling.

Here's a quote from TFA

> See, we were founded in 2019, making us a pre-AI company (ew!).

I dunno. Maybe the value is in the data siphon from gullible companies trusting Hex with their data.
It's like they asked an AI to throw together every possible flourish into a single page.
Darn, i liked their old site better
I’ve seen this terrible mix of sans serif and serif italics in titles from /frontend-design one too many times. What the hell is with that?
the model didn't just invent those design elements without training data.

Definitely unhinged, but in a somewhat interesting way. It's like they made "AI slop" into a design language and decided to play with it. You can easily tell when a website is low-effort one-shot Claude output, and this isn't that.
As much as I hate to say it, did anyone ever care beyond a few employees? Get rid of them and well..

I liked Hex. I introduced it to my company and now it has become the main BI tool.

However, since they started pushing the whole AI thing I no longer like them.

It may speed up doing analytics, but makes everything hard to maintain, creates a ton of duplication and adds yet another layer to take care of.

I also think AI may come back to bite them in the ass. What's the point of an analytics platform is you can create dashboards from scratch directly using AI. What are they adding to the table?

They should have stuck to just making developers lives easier instead of that weird objective that is trying to make analytics accessible for everyone

Its the same conundrum any BI tool is going to have (sigma, tableau, redash)

likely they focus on something orthogonal, like trust and security, permissions, etc

fwiw i work at one of their 'top customers' and found their ai to be really useful for spinning up basically ephemeral dashboards for anyone to use (aka, i dont need to file a request to the data team and wait for someone to get back to me or go back and forth). i just ask it to do the thing.

The reliable layer that captures the data. That is what they bring to the table. For now.

Once AI can orchestrate and maintain a project with dozens of clients without slipping, they will be relegated to non-technical SMBs - many enterprises would just build their own shit. No contracts to sign. Full control. AI hosts and maintains. Great.

Then they might pivot to security (heck I would if I were in any SaaS business today).

> Once AI can orchestrate and maintain a project with dozens of clients without slipping, they will be relegated to non-technical SMBs - many enterprises would just build their own shit. No contracts to sign. Full control. AI hosts and maintains. Great.

The problem with this is that, as of today, no AI company will give you support if the AI generated product doesn't work, at least no company I know of. When we pay for a software product, we mostly pay for the support and accountability transfer to the provider.

I mean at least that's what we used to do. Nowadays support and software quality are so bad that maybe one should just vibe code everything. So I think I've come around to your opinion while writing this comment lol.

We are heavy Hex users at OpenRouter. I was skeptical that it would replace "core" reporting tools like Looker, but the efficacy of the Hex agent has made it our go-to for just about all of our analytics, and allowed us to get incredibly far with a single (very good) person on the data team.

We can make completely reproducible reporting when we need it (for e.g. our weekly business reviews), while the agent can answer all of the ad-hoc stuff that would normally be done by a small army of analysts scurrying around.

OpenRouter only having 1 person in the data team is completely nuts. A canary in the coal mine for whats to come in the whole data space :|

1 or 2 exceptional ICs, a clean semantic layer and agents is "all you need".

RIP to the sexiest job of the 21st century ...

Writing has been on the wall since before LLMs took over. Companies invested an incredible amount of money into "big data" over the past 15 years, and the returns are still nowhere to be seen. Data science and data engineering departments have been among the most impacted in all the layoff waves since covid.

As far as I know OpenRouter has <100 employees, maybe even <50.

1-2% headcount on data is below average for a tech company but not unbelievable either.

It is true you can get a lot further than before with "just" a clean semantic layer though!
The secret here is that building the semantic layer is a ton of work, predominantly done by data people.
Far less promising companies with zero profits often have thousands more employees…

It was always a pointless job. I’d watch data people manually put together PowerPoints by hand when it’s the same powerpoint every week and could be entirely automatic.

But they don’t, because they want to look busy. And it’s not like they actually understand the data anyway, because they’ve never worked in the area the data comes from.

thanks for sharing.

any other tools that are also key to your stack that you wouldn't mind sharing, so others can learn from and try out?

Was it when B2B marketing realized that engineers equated "native" with "best/fastest/simplest solution available"? Or is it even more stupid than that?

Native already had very specific meaning to technologists. Seems to me the industry is trading on the existing credibility of "things that are native"

I also hate them, along with “go to market” and “customer focused”.
